title: Computability of entropic query-size bounds
area: Database theory and finite model theory
formal:
Is the logarithmic entropic query-size bound uniformly computable? More precisely, does a single deterministic Turing machine, given any finite set of degree constraints \(\mathcal D=\{(X_i,Y_i,b_i):1\leq i\leq k\}\) on \([n]\) with nonnegative rational logarithmic budgets, and any \(m\in\mathbb N\), halt and output either \(+\infty\) when \(E(\mathcal D)=+\infty\), or a rational \(q\) satisfying \(|q-E(\mathcal D)|\leq 2^{-m}\) when
\[E(\mathcal D)=\sup\{h([n]):h\in\overline{\Gamma_n^*},\ h(Y_i)-h(X_i)\leq b_i\ (1\leq i\leq k)\}<+\infty?\]
Here \(\overline{\Gamma_n^*}\) is the closure of the discrete entropy region defined below; \(n\) is part of the input.
why: The strongest information-theoretic query estimates are useful algorithmically only if their numerical values can be obtained effectively. A computability theorem would make this extremal use of arbitrary discrete distributions accessible to uniform algorithms; a noncomputability theorem would identify a fundamental limit on exact information-theoretic database estimation, even with unlimited running time.
status_note: The 2022 seminar asks Question 7.1. Mengel–Romashchenko v1, 27 August 2026, abstract and introduction explicitly say that general entropic-bound computability is not known. A bounded primary-source check on 16 September 2026 found no matching resolution; cited results were read for their statements and scope, not independently proved.

progress.text: Hung Ngo poses computability of the entropic bound as Question 7.1 at Seminar 22301; the report appears in February 2023.

Suciu’s expanded paper gives the cone and duality framework; Theorem 9.7 identifies the entropic upper value with optimization over the almost-entropic closure. It does not provide a general computation procedure.
Im, Moseley, Ngo and Pruhs give a polynomial-size formulation for simple degree constraints, providing a tractable case of the coincident bounds.
Mengel and Romashchenko explicitly retain general entropic-bound computability as unknown while obtaining new results for acyclic constraints and projections.

sentences: Entropy bounds limit the number of tuples returned by a database join from constraints on conditional degrees.
The entropic bound optimizes total entropy over the closure of all finite discrete entropy vectors.
The question asks for one terminating algorithm that computes this value to every requested absolute accuracy in arbitrary dimension.
Simple constraints admit effective special cases, while the general polymatroid relaxation can overestimate the desired value.
Resolving computability would determine whether the strongest information-theoretic estimate is accessible to algorithms at all.

definitions:
Let \(n\geq1\), \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and \(2^{[n]}\) be its set of subsets. Given jointly distributed discrete random variables \(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n\), each with a finite alphabet, their entropy vector is the real set function
\[h(S)=H(Z_S)=-\sum_z\Pr[Z_S=z]\log_2\Pr[Z_S=z],\qquad h(\varnothing)=0,\]
where \(Z_S\) is the tuple with indices in \(S\), and \(0\log_2 0=0\). Alphabets and real joint probabilities are unrestricted. The set of all such vectors is \(\Gamma_n^*\). Its closure \(\overline{\Gamma_n^*}\) in the finite-dimensional Euclidean space of subset coordinates consists of all limits of sequences of entropy vectors and is the almost-entropic cone. Neither alphabet sizes nor convergence rates are input bounds. Continuous differential entropy is not used.

A degree constraint is a triple \((X,Y,b)\), where \(X\subseteq Y\subseteq[n]\) and \(b\in\mathbb Q_{\geq0}\). It bounds the conditional entropy \(h(Y)-h(X)\). The case \(X=\varnothing\) gives a cardinality-type constraint, and \(b=0\) gives a functional dependency. Equal sets, repeated triples and an empty list are permitted. The all-zero entropy vector is always feasible, so the supremum is in \([0,+\infty]\). The optimization is over the closed almost-entropic cone, not just the nonclosed set of entropy vectors satisfying the constraints exactly; this distinction matters on faces defined by zero budgets.

For a database interpretation, a full conjunctive query returns the natural join of finite relations: an output tuple assigns all variables and its projection onto each relation's columns is present in that relation. There are no duplicate output tuples and no existentially projected variables. A bound of \(N\) on the number of extensions from columns \(X\) to columns \(Y\) gives the entropy budget \(b=\log_2 N\). Drawing a join tuple uniformly makes its full entropy the logarithm of the join size. The quantity \(2^{E(\mathcal D)}\) is the information-theoretic upper bound; the question asks to compute its logarithm, rather than to enumerate joins or compute the exact maximum size of a finite database instance.

The finite encoding used here writes \(n\) and the list length in unary, every subset as an \(n\)-bit mask, and each rational budget as a nonnegative binary numerator and a positive binary denominator, with delimiters. The precision \(m\) is given in unary. This is an explicit rational logarithmic-budget version of the source's numerical problem, with no real-number oracle. At the level of computability it also covers positive integer degree bounds supplied as \(N\): cone homogeneity handles rational budgets by scaling them to integer logarithms, while positive values \(\log_2 N\) can be bracketed multiplicatively by rational numbers, keeping zero budgets exactly zero. This equivalence concerns computability, not polynomial-time equivalence of the two encodings.

Unbounded inputs are included. They can be recognized by starting with \(S=\varnothing\) and repeatedly adjoining \(Y_i\) whenever \(X_i\subseteq S\). The optimum is finite exactly when the resulting closure is \([n]\). In that case conditional-entropy inequalities and subadditivity supply an explicit finite upper bound. If some variables remain outside, let them all share an arbitrarily high-entropy random variable and make the other variables constant; every constraint is satisfied while the objective is unbounded. Thus recognizing infinity is not the unknown part of the problem.

The machine must halt on every valid input, with a finite binary rational output in the bounded case; malformed strings may be rejected. There is no time or space bound, no advice, oracle, fixed dimension or randomness. Accuracy is absolute in base-two entropy units. In particular the machine must achieve error at most \(1/100\), by taking \(m=7\), and also every finer requested accuracy. A one-sided sequence of estimates without a computable error guarantee does not suffice.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that the displayed uniform machine exists, or that it does not. An affirmative proof must provide an effective procedure and prove termination and the requested two-sided absolute error for every finite dimension, rational degree-constraint list and precision, including zero budgets and the stated infinity convention. A negative proof must establish noncomputability of this particular functional, not merely undecidability of a different entropy-region membership or information-inequality problem. An exact symbolic formula is unnecessary, while a computable value for each separately fixed input without one uniform procedure is insufficient. There are no unproved complexity assumptions in the target.

source_formulation.text: Does an algorithm compute the entropic bound on query output size from the supplied constraints?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of Question 7.1; entropy closure, numerical representation and accuracy are made explicit in this card.

context_blocks.text: The seminar groups several algorithmic questions about information-theoretic database bounds. Question 7.1 asks for computability of the entropic bound; Question 7.2 separately asks about the complexity of its polymatroid relaxation. The first issue is whether any terminating numerical algorithm exists, before asking whether one is efficient.

Entropy inequalities constrain correlations among columns in a join. Using every valid inequality gives a potentially sharper bound than the familiar Shannon inequalities alone. Suciu formulates the entropic upper bound by such inequalities and identifies its value with optimization over the closed almost-entropic cone. This closure specifies which limiting entropy vectors belong to the target.

Replacing the almost-entropic cone by normalized monotone submodular set functions gives a finite linear program, with exponentially many subset coordinates. This yields a computable upper relaxation, but a gap between that relaxation and the entropic optimum prevents it from settling the question. Restricting alphabet sizes also changes the feasible region unless a sufficient effective approximation theorem is proved.

For simple degree constraints, where every conditioning set has size at most one, the entropic and polymatroid bounds coincide and a polynomial-size linear program is available. This tractable subclass does not cover arbitrary conditioning sets or all zero-budget functional dependencies.

Mengel and Romashchenko still describe general computability as unresolved in August 2026. Their new work examines acyclic dependencies and shows that allowing projected variables can create gaps between entropy and polymatroid bounds. That result concerns the comparison of bounds in a richer query setting, not an algorithm or impossibility proof for the full general numerical target here.
